relevant_findings.topic: Porch floor RP scope — existing painted/coated porch and portico floor surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: Porch floor repaint covers previously coated exterior porch, portico, and covered patio floor surfaces. Two substrate types: (1) Concrete porch floors previously painted with porch enamel or sealed with acrylic sealer. (2) Wood tongue-and-groove porch floors previously painted with porch enamel. The primary RP driver is foot traffic wear — walking surfaces degrade from top-down abrasion unlike vertical surfaces that fail from weathering. Assessment of existing coating condition (sound through peeling) drives prep intensity. Coating system is NOT a configuration dimension for RP — porch enamel is the standard repaint product for both substrates (original coating system variation collapsed to single repaint path).

relevant_findings.topic: Quality tier QT2-QT3 — utilitarian walking surface
relevant_findings.finding: Porch floors are utilitarian walking surfaces. QT2 (economy — single finish coat, minimal prep) and QT3 (standard — 2 finish coats, full prep) cover the realistic range. QT4/QT5 are not applicable — nobody specifies gallery-grade finish on a porch floor. QT2 is valid because some customers want basic refreshment only (one coat touch-up on sound existing). QT3 is the standard repaint (full prep + 2 finish coats).
relevant_findings.source: Field convention; porch floor is utilitarian, not decorative

relevant_findings.topic: Existing coating condition is the primary RP cost driver
relevant_findings.finding: Four condition states drive prep labor: (1) Sound — existing coating intact, light scuff sand for adhesion. (2) Worn — traffic wear-through in high-traffic paths (doorway approach, stair landing), moderate sand/feather. (3) Failing — adhesion loss, flaking in patches, moderate-to-heavy scraping. (4) Peeling — sheet delamination, typically moisture-driven from below, heavy scraping or chemical strip. On porch floors, 'worn' is the most common repaint trigger — concentrated foot traffic creates visible wear paths while surrounding areas remain sound.
relevant_findings.source: Exterior_Weathering_Surface_Assessment_Doctrine.md; field convention for horizontal traffic surfaces

relevant_findings.topic: Concrete porch RP prep — NO acid etch, use chemical degloss or mechanical abrasion
relevant_findings.finding: Concrete porch floors being repainted do NOT get acid etched (that is NC prep for bare concrete). RP prep on painted concrete: (1) Sound/worn: chemical degloss (liquid sander/deglosser) or mechanical scuff with floor buffer and abrasive pad. (2) Failing/peeling: scrape loose paint, feather-edge sand, chemical degloss remaining. No profiling needed — existing coating provides adhesion base. Acid etch would damage existing sound coating areas.

relevant_findings.topic: Wood porch RP prep — sand existing, feather edges at wear areas
relevant_findings.finding: Wood tongue-and-groove porch floors being repainted: (1) Sound: light scuff sand (120-150 grit) for adhesion. (2) Worn: sand wear-through areas to feather edge, prime bare wood spots. (3) Failing/peeling: scrape loose paint, sand to feather, prime all bare areas. T&G joints may need brush-back to work primer into joint grooves. MC verification still required (<15%) but not the 3-6 month seasoning of NC.

relevant_findings.topic: Moisture underneath — substructure moisture is the primary porch floor failure mode
relevant_findings.finding: Porch floors over crawl spaces or open substructure experience moisture migration from below. This is the #1 cause of porch floor paint peeling. Assessment must include underside moisture check — if moisture is migrating through slab or wood subfloor, coating will fail regardless of prep quality. For concrete: calcium chloride test (ASTM F1869) if peeling pattern suggests moisture. For wood: pin-type MC meter on underside if accessible. Moisture-driven peeling is a HARD STOP for standard repaint — ventilation/drainage correction needed before repainting.

relevant_findings.topic: Non-slip additive — mandatory for all porch floor RP
relevant_findings.finding: Anti-slip aggregate (silica sand for flat areas, aluminum oxide for steps) is mandatory for all porch floor repaint coats just as for NC. Broadcast into wet first coat or mixed into final coat. This is a safety requirement for exterior horizontal walking surfaces, not optional. Customer communication about texture change from original (if original lacked grit) is important.

relevant_findings.topic: Furniture removal and cure time — customer impact on occupied porch
relevant_findings.finding: Porch furniture must be moved off the work surface. This is a fixed-time task that varies with furnishing density. Cure time is critical: porch floor enamel needs 48-72 hours before foot traffic (7 days for heavy furniture). Customer must be informed of restricted access period. Alternate entry path planning may be needed if the porch is the primary home entrance.
relevant_findings.source: Field convention; manufacturer TDS cure schedules

relevant_findings.topic: Threshold transitions — critical tape line at porch-to-interior junction
relevant_findings.finding: Where porch floor meets door threshold and interior flooring, a clean tape line is mandatory. The porch floor coating must terminate at the threshold edge — no coating on threshold metal or interior floor. This is a high-visibility detail that drives customer satisfaction. Brush-cut at threshold, not rolled.

relevant_findings.topic: Application methods — brush_roll primary, spray_backroll for larger porches
relevant_findings.finding: brush_roll is the primary application method for porch floor RP. Roller for field area, brush for edges, threshold details, railing base details, and T&G joint back-brushing on wood. spray_backroll is viable for larger porches (>400 SF) where spray efficiency justifies masking overhead. Spray-only is PROHIBITED on porch floors — backroll required for proper film build and aggregate embedment on horizontal surfaces.

relevant_findings.topic: Porch enamel is the universal RP finish product
relevant_findings.finding: Regardless of what the original coating was (porch enamel, concrete stain, acrylic sealer), the standard RP product is acrylic porch & floor enamel (satin). It provides the best combination of adhesion over existing coatings, abrasion resistance, and slip-resistance aggregate compatibility. Original polyurea or epoxy coatings are excluded from standard RP scope — those require specialty contractor. Original concrete stain can be overcoated with porch enamel after proper prep and bonding primer.

relevant_findings.topic: Spot prime vs full prime on RP — condition-driven
relevant_findings.finding: Primer strategy on RP: (1) Sound/worn on concrete: no primer needed if existing coating is sound — direct recoat with porch enamel after degloss. (2) Sound/worn on wood: spot prime bare wear-through areas only. (3) Failing on either substrate: spot prime all scraped-bare areas. (4) Peeling: full prime after heavy scrape — too much bare substrate for spot priming. Bonding primer (e.g., Stix) required when recoating over unknown or incompatible existing coatings.

Porch steps (tread + riser per step) are a conditional scope component. Some porches have steps, some are at grade. Steps require brush application (roller cannot reach riser face), alternating-step pattern for access during cure, and aluminum oxide anti-slip aggregate (harder grit for high-wear step nosing). Step count is EA-based.

Temperature, humidity, wind, and sun exposure are NOT estimatable — unpredictable at bid time. Excluded per PaintFactor OS RC-003. Scheduling constraints (48-72hr cure before traffic) are communicated but not modeled as estimation modifiers.

research_corrections.original_claim: Coating system should be a configuration dimension for RP
research_corrections.corrected_to: Coating system is NOT a configuration dimension for RP. All RP uses porch enamel regardless of original coating. Original polyurea/epoxy excluded from RP scope entirely.
research_corrections.source: Field convention — RP converges on single product

research_corrections.corrected_to: Environmental conditions are NOT estimatable — excluded per PaintFactor OS RC-003.

includes: Moisture testing for concrete substrates (when peeling pattern suggests moisture)
Chemical degloss or mechanical abrasion for sound/worn concrete
Scraping and feather-edge sanding for failing/peeling
Spot prime bare areas (failing) or full prime (peeling)
Bonding primer for incompatible existing coatings
Porch & floor enamel application — 2 coats (brush_roll or spray_backroll)
Anti-slip aggregate broadcast into wet first coat
Step/riser painting (conditional — brush only, alternating pattern)
Wall base, railing base, landscape, hardscape protection
Customer communication: 48-72hr cure before foot traffic
